# Week 5, Day 5.1 - Prerequisites check

Today is about locators that keep working. The TypeScript is about reading data out of objects
and knowing when the compiler stops helping you.

| Concept | Taught in |
|---|---|
| `import x from "file.json"` | [week4/day4_2](/learn/w4/d4/p2) |
| `readFileSync` + `JSON.parse` | [week4/day4_1](/learn/w4/d4/p1) |
| `Object.entries` | new - below, on top of [week4/day4_1](/learn/w4/d4/p1) |
| `any` and why `as` is not a check | new - below |

**Next:** [Day 5.2 - Locators that survive](/learn/w5/d5/p2)

## Concept 1 - `Object.entries`

In [week4/day4_1](/learn/w4/d4/p1) you destructured `[i, value]` pairs out of an array's
`.entries()`. `Object.entries` is the same shape for an **object**: it hands back `[key, value]`
pairs, so you can loop over something that has names instead of positions.

You will use it to check every selector in a JSON file at once.

// Typing beats reading. Peek above if you get stuck.

## Concept 2 - `any` switches the compiler off

`JSON.parse` returns `any`. Anything typed `any` accepts every property access without complaint
- including the ones that do not exist.

| Expression | Type | Typo caught? |
|---|---|---|
| `import L from "./l.json"; L.login.emialBox` | inferred from the file | **yes, at compile time** |
| `JSON.parse(s).login.emialBox` | `any` | no - `undefined` at run time |

This decides which of the two loading styles you should use, so it is not a detail.

// Your turn — retype the example above from memory, then run it.
// Typing beats reading. Peek above if you get stuck.

## Concept 3 - `as` asserts, it does not check

`JSON.parse(raw) as Config` tells the compiler *trust me*. Nothing is verified at run time - if
the file's shape is different, you get `undefined` exactly as before, only now with autocomplete
lying to you about it.

| Tool | Checks at compile time | Checks at run time |
|---|---|---|
| `import` a JSON file | **yes** | n/a - the shape is the file |
| `as SomeType` | no - it silences the compiler | **no** |
| A validator (zod, ajv) | yes | **yes** |

**Next:** [Day 5.2 - Locators that survive](/learn/w5/d5/p2)

# Week 5, Day 5.2 - Locators that survive

A suite that passed in March fails in June with nobody having touched it. Two causes account for
most of it: **whitespace moved**, and **a second element appeared with the same name**.

Both are demonstrated below on the real app, with the fix measured rather than asserted.

> **Mode: test-runner.** This part is about running specs with the Playwright test runner. The studio editor runs library code, so follow these along in your own checkout.

## Step 1 - whitespace, and `normalize-space()` A developer reformats a template. The rendered text looks identical; the markup now reads: ```html

Pay Bills

``` | Locator | Matches? | |---|---| | `//p[text()="Pay Bills"]` | **no** - `text()` compares the raw string | | `//p[normalize-space()="Pay Bills"]` | **yes** | | `getByText("Pay Bills", { exact: true })` | **yes** | | `text="Pay Bills"` | **yes** | `normalize-space()` trims both ends and collapses every run of whitespace to one space, *then* compares. The row that should change your habits is the third: **Playwright's own text locators already normalize.** `normalize-space()` is a fix for a problem XPath has and `getByText` does not.

## Step 2 - the second failure: a duplicate name

Sign in to the banking app and count the dashboard tiles: **12 tiles, and "Statements" appears
twice.**

`getByText("Statements", { exact: true })` matches 2 elements. You saw this failure in
[week3/day1_2](/learn/w3/d1/p2), where the point was *how fast* it fails compared with a
timeout. Here the point is what to do about it.

Matching 2 is fine to count and fine to assert on. Clicking is what fails:

```
Error: strict mode violation: getByText('Statements', { exact: true })
       resolved to 2 elements
```

**Strict mode is a feature.** The alternative - silently acting on whichever element came first
in the DOM - is a test that passes while checking the wrong thing.

## Step 3 - the fix that does not work here

The standard advice is *narrow by the parent*. On this page it fails: both `Statements` tiles sit
in a `div.card-body.text-color` inside a `div.col-md-8`. Identical ancestors, so the parent tells
them apart not at all - `page.locator("div.card-body").getByText("Statements")` still matches 2.

Worth knowing that the textbook answer can miss, and worth checking rather than assuming.

## Step 4 - the fixes that do work

| Fix | Code | Honest verdict |
|---|---|---|
| Go further up | `page.locator(".card").first().getByText("Statements")` | best here - 3 cards, the two tiles are in different ones |
| Pick by position | `page.locator("p.card-text").nth(3)` | works; breaks the moment a tile is inserted above |
| `.first()` | `...getByText("Statements").first()` | silences the error without deciding anything |

That last one deserves its reputation. `.first()` makes the test pass whichever of the two it
lands on - which means it stopped checking. It is the fix you reach for at 6pm and regret in
review.

// Your turn — retype the example above from memory, then run it.
// Typing beats reading. Peek above if you get stuck.

## Step 5 - the ranking worth memorising

| Prefer | Why |
|---|---|
| `getByRole`, `getByLabel` | tied to what the control *is*; also normalizes whitespace |
| `getByTestId` | changes only when someone means to change it |
| `getByText` | good, but text is translated and reworded |
| CSS on a semantic class | survives layout changes, dies with a redesign |
| XPath by position (`//div[3]/p[2]`) | records where things sit today |

Every locator is a bet about what will not change. The list is ordered by how good the bet is.

# Week 5, Day 5.3 - Externalised locators, and their cost

The next thing teams try after POM: move every selector into a JSON file, so a non-programmer can
fix one without touching TypeScript.

It works. It also costs more than people expect, and this lesson measures both.

> **Mode: test-runner.** This part is about running specs with the Playwright test runner. The studio editor runs library code, so follow these along in your own checkout.

## Step 1 - the file

```json
{
  "login":     { "emailBox": "...", "passwordBox": "...", "loginButton": "#login" },
  "dashboard": { "tile": "p.card-text", "card": ".card", "logoutButton": "button.btn-primary" }
}
```

Every selector the suite depends on, in one place you can read in ten seconds. That is a real
benefit and not a small one.

> Both of those `button.btn-primary` and `#login` values were **checked against the live page**
> before being written down. My first draft guessed `button.logout-btn` - it matches zero
> elements. A locator file full of plausible guesses is worse than no file, because it looks
> authoritative.

## Step 2 - a test that checks the file itself

Step 2 of that spec loops over every entry with `Object.entries` and asserts each one still
matches something.

Worth having for real. An externalised selector that quietly stops matching is invisible until
some unrelated test fails for a confusing reason; this test names the dead key instead.

```ts
for (const [key, selector] of Object.entries(LOCATORS.login)) {
  await expect(page.locator(selector), `login.${key} -> ${selector}`).toHaveCount(1);
}
```

The second argument to `expect` is the message shown on failure - which is what turns *a test
failed* into *`login.loginButton` is dead*.

## Step 3 - the cost, measured

Two ways to load the same file:

```ts
import LOCATORS from "./day5-locators.json";                       // A
const LOCATORS = JSON.parse(readFileSync(p, "utf-8"));             // B
```

Now make a typo - `LOCATORS.login.emialBox`:

| | A: `import` | B: `JSON.parse` |
|---|---|---|
| `npx tsc --noEmit` | **error TS2551: Property 'emialBox' does not exist... Did you mean 'emailBox'?** | passes |
| At run time | never gets there | `undefined`, then a confusing locator error |

Verified with the compiler, not assumed. Prefer A - it needs `"resolveJsonModule": true` in
`tsconfig.json`, already set in this repo.

And note what A does *not* give you: the compiler checks the **key**, never the selector. Both
styles will happily hand Playwright a selector that matches nothing. Only Step 2's test catches
that.

// Typing beats reading. Peek above if you get stuck.

## Step 4 - so should you externalise?

| Externalise when | Keep it in the page class when |
|---|---|
| A non-programmer really will edit the file | it is developers all the way down |
| Selectors differ per environment or per tenant | one app, one DOM |
| A generator produces them | humans write them |

For most teams: **a page class already gives you one-place-to-edit**, plus autocomplete, rename
refactoring, and a compiler that catches typos. JSON trades all three away for editability by
someone who, in practice, is rarely the one editing it.

Ask who the file is for. If the answer is "it seemed tidier", keep the class.

## Step 5 - what actually makes a suite survive

Nothing on this list is a Playwright feature.

| Practice | Effect |
|---|---|
| One name for one thing (page class or JSON key) | a markup change is one edit |
| Prefer role and label locators | fewer bets on things that change |
| A test over your own locator file | dead selectors get named, not hunted |
| Fail loudly on ambiguity (strict mode) | never a test that passes while checking nothing |
| Delete tests nobody reads | the cheapest maintenance there is |

# Week 5, Day 5.4 - Practice

Work in `week5/generated/`. Copy `day5-locators.json` before editing it.

The last two problems close out the week rather than the day.

## Week 5 done

| Day | You can now |
|---|---|
| 1 | run one suite two ways, from two configs, and say which setting wins |
| 2 | sign in once per run and prove the saved session is doing the work |
| 3 | name the Page Object Model's three rules and why rule 3 pays |
| 4 | hand out page objects as fixtures, including worker-scoped ones |
| 5 | pick locators that survive, and decide whether to externalise them |

problems.statement:
**Find the third duplicate**
The dashboard has 12 tiles and "Statements" twice. Find out whether any other label repeats.

**Right when:** you can print each label with its count, and say how many are ambiguous.

**Click the second Statements**
Click the *second* `Statements` tile, deliberately, three different ways: `.nth()`, narrowing by
`.card`, and one more of your choosing.

**Right when:** all three reach the same page, and you can rank them by how long each will keep
working.

**Whitespace, on purpose**
Use `page.setContent` to build markup with a newline inside a button's label. Find a locator that
matches and one that does not.

**Right when:** you have one of each, and can say which of the two you would have written before
this lesson.

**Break your locator file**
Change one selector in your copy of the JSON to something that matches nothing. Run the spec.

**Right when:** the Step 2 test fails and its message names the dead key - not a generic timeout.

**Prove the compiler difference**
Add `LOCATORS.login.emialBox` to a spec, run `npx tsc --noEmit`. Then do the same through
`JSON.parse`.

**Right when:** you can paste both results - one error, one silence.

**A locator file for your PayBillsPage**
Externalise the selectors from your Day 3.4 `PayBillsPage` into JSON, then argue the other side:
write two sentences on why keeping them in the class would have been better.

**Right when:** it runs, and your two sentences name a specific thing you gave up.

**Week 5, end to end**
Build one run that uses every day of this week: a `@smoke`-tagged spec, driven through your page
objects and fixtures, launched by its own config, with `storageState` skipping the login.

**Right when:** `npm run` style single command, no flags, correct test count - and you can name
which lesson each piece came from.

**The honest review**
Take the suite you just built and find its weakest locator. Not the ugliest - the one most likely
to break first.

**Right when:** you can say what change to the app would break it, and what you would replace it
with. If nothing looks fragile, you have not looked hard enough at the CSS ones.
